problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{36 -(3x - 2)^2}} \, \textrm{d}x.$
solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{36-(3x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{36(1-(3x-2)^{2}/36)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{36}\cdot \sqrt{1-(3x-2)^{2}/36}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{6\sqrt{1-(3x-2)^{2}/36}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3x-2)^{2}/36}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((3x-2)/6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u + C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{3x-2}{6}\right).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=\dfrac{3x-2}{6}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{36-(3x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((3x-2)/6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{3x-2}{6})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(2x-3)^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{4((2x-3)^{2}/4+1)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+(2x-3)^{2}/4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+((2x-3)/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{2x-3}{2}).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=\frac{2x-3}{2}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(2x-3)^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+((2x-3)/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2x-3}{2})+C\end{aligned}
$$

problem: What is $\displaystyle \int(1)/(\sqrt{4 - (2x + 1)^{2}})dx$?
What is $\displaystyle \int(4)/(\mid x + 5 \mid \sqrt{(x + 5)^{2} - 1})dx$?

solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4-(6x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4(1-(6x+1)^{2}/4)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{1-(6x+1)^{2}/4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-(6x+1)^{2}/4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(6x+1)^{2}/4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((6x+1)/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{6x+1}{2}).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=\frac{6x+1}{2}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4-(6x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((6x+1)/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{6x+1}{2})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|x-3|\sqrt{(x-3)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|x-3|\sqrt{(x-3)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x-3).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=x-3.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|x-3|\sqrt{(x-3)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|x-3|\sqrt{(x-3)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(x-3)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{|2x-7|\sqrt{(2x-7)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{|2x-7|\sqrt{(2x-7)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(2x-7).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=2x-7.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{|2x-7|\sqrt{(2x-7)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{|2x-7|\sqrt{(2x-7)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(2x-7)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|x+1|\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|x+1|\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x+1).$

So, let's perform the substitution 

$$
u=x+1.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|x+1|\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|x+1|\sqrt{(x+1)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =2\,\text{arcsec}(x+1)+C\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{x^2-2x + 3}\, \textrm{d}x.$
solution:
First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^2-2x + 3
& = x^2 - 2 \cdot x+ (1^2 - 1^2) + 3 \\[3pt]
& = (x^2 - 2 \cdot x+ 1^2) - 1 + 3 \\[3pt]
& = (x-1)^2+2
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-2x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-1)^{2}+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-1)/\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u
=
\arctan u + C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{x-1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$.

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\dfrac{x-1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \sqrt{2}\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u$, and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-2x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-1)/\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{2}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+7 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+({2}^{2}-{2}^{2})+7 \\  & =({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})-4+7 \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-4x+7}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-2)/\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{3}}).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-4x+7}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-2)/\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{3}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle \int_{-2}^{\sqrt{3} - 3}\frac{8}{x^{2} + 6x + 10}dx$.

solution:
First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-6x+18 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+({3}^{2}-{3}^{2})+18 \\  & =({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})-9+18 \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+9\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-6x+18}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-3)^{2}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-3)/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x-3}{3}).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x-3}{3}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-6x+18}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+((x-3)/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x-3}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{3}^{3+\sqrt{3}}\frac{5}{{x}^{2}-6x+10}\,\text{d}x.$
solution:
First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-6x+10 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+({3}^{2}-{3}^{2})+10 \\  & =({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})-9+10 \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{{x}^{2}-6x+10}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{5}{(x-3)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{1+(x-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x-3)$.

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x-3.
$$

 
Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u$.

| $x$ | $3$ | $3+\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u$, and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{3+\sqrt{3}}\frac{5}{{x}^{2}-6x+10}\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{3}^{3+\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{1+(x-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =5\operatorname{arctan}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =5(\operatorname{arctan}⁡\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0) \\  & =5(\frac{\pi }{3}-0) \\  & =5(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+10 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+({3}^{2}-{3}^{2})+10 \\  & =({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})-9+10 \\  & =(x+3)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{6}{{x}^{2}+6x+10}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{6}{(x+3)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\int \frac{1}{1+(x+3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x+3).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x+3.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-3$ | $\sqrt{3}-3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{\sqrt{3}-3}\frac{6}{{x}^{2}+6x+10}\,\text{d}x & =6{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\operatorname{arctan}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =6(\operatorname{arctan}⁡\sqrt{3}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)) \\  & =6(\frac{\pi }{3}-0) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+5 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+({2}^{2}-{2}^{2})+5 \\  & =({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})-4+5 \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+1\end{aligned}

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$

problem: Calculate ${\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4x - 4x^2}} \, \textrm{d}x}.$
solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-4{x}^{2} & =-(4{x}^{2}-4x) \\  & =-((2x)^{2}-2\cdot 2x+1-1) \\  & =-((2x-1)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(2x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4x-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x-1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(2x - 1).$  

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u =2x - 1.
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \dfrac12\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{4x-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x-1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{-13/2}^{-11/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-12x-35}}\,\text{d}x.$
solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-12x-35 & =-({x}^{2}+12x+35) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 6x+[{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}]+35) \\  & =-((x+6)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x+6)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
{\int }_{-13/2}^{-11/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-12x-35}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-13/2}^{-11/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x+6.$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x+6.
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-13/2$ | $-11/2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-1/2$ | $1/2$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-13/2}^{-11/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-12x-35}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-13/2}^{-11/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+6)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle{\int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{x^2-2x}}\, \textrm{d}x}.$
solution:
First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    x^2-2x&= x^2 -2x +(1-1)\\[3pt]
              &= (x^2 -2x +1)-1\\[3pt]
         &= (x-1)^2-1
         
  \end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get

$$
\int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{x^2-2x}}\, \textrm{d}x 
= \int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{(x-1)^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \, \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec} \, u +C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x-1$.

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x-1.
$$

 
Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u$.

| $x$ | $1+\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ | $2$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{x^2-2x}}\, \textrm{d}x 
&=  \int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3}\dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{(x-1)^2-1}}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt]
&=\int_{2/\sqrt{3}}^{2} \dfrac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt]
&=  \textrm{arcsec}\, {u}\Big|_{2/\sqrt{3}}^{2}\\[5pt]
&= \textrm{arcsec} \left(2\right)  - \textrm{arcsec}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \right)\\[5pt]
&=\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}.

\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Consider the following integral:

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{x^2+2x+5}\, \textrm{d}x
$$

This integral doesn't resemble any of the standard integrals we have encountered so far.

However, notice that we can complete the square in the denominator as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x+5 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot x+5 \\  & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot x+({1}^{2}-{1}^{2})+5 \\  & =({x}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot x+{1}^{2})-{1}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x+1)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug the above into our integral and collect a factor of ${\color{red}{4}}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x+5}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{4[(x+1)^{2}/4+1]}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}/4+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+(x+1)^{2}/4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+((x+1)/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this now resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u = \arctan u + C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{x+1}{2}\right).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\dfrac{x+1}{2}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x+5}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+((x+1)/2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}(\frac{x+1}{2})+C\end{aligned}
$$

And we're done!
Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is $x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 6y = 12.$
solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x+6y & =12 \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+({y}^{2}+6y) & =12 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y+{3}^{2}) & =12+{2}^{2}+{3}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y+{3}^{2}) & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+(y+3)^{2} & ={5}^{2} \\ (x-2)^{2}+(y-(-3))^{2} & ={5}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(2,-3)$ and its radius is $5.$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-4x+2{y}^{2}-y & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}y & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2x)+({y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}y) & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot x+{1}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{4}y+{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}) & =-\frac{1}{2}+{1}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot x+{1}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{4}y+{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}) & =\frac{9}{16}\end{aligned}

$$

problem:

Clearly, this is a circle of radius $3$ centered at $(1,2)$. But how can we determine the center and radius from the given circle equation?

$$

$$

By grouping the $x$ and $y$ terms and completing the squares, we can write the equation in the standard form

$$
(x-a)^2 + (y-b)^2 = r^2.
$$

We carry out the process with the following steps:

**Step 1.** Group the $x$ and $y$ terms.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2x-4y & =4 \\ ({x}^{2}-2x)+({y}^{2}-4y) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** In each group, add the square of half the linear coefficient to both sides of the equation. 

- Here, the $x$ coefficient is $-2$, so we add $\left( \dfrac{-2}{2} \right)^2 = (-1)^2 = 1$ to both sides.

- Likewise, the $y$ coefficient is $-4$, so we add $\left( \dfrac{-4}{2} \right)^2 = (-2)^2 = 4$ to both sides.

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}-2x+1)+({y}^{2}-4y+4) & =4+1+4 \\ ({x}^{2}-2x+1)+({y}^{2}-4y+4) & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Finally, we factor each group into a perfect square, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =9 \\ (x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & ={3}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can see that the equation represents a circle centered at $(1,2)$ with radius $3$.

\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}-8x & =-4({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-4({x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =-4[(x+1)^{2}-1] \\  & =4[1-(x+1)^{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{4[1-(x+1)^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: $\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x=$
solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-{x}^{2}-3 & =-({x}^{2}-4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: $\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x=$
solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x & =-({x}^{2}+4x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{4-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2(x+2)\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+2}{2})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+2}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+2}{2})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+2}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x+2}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: $\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x=$
solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-6x & =-({x}^{2}+6x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) \\  & =-((x+3)^{2}-9) \\  & =9-(x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{9-{(x+3)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{9-9{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{3}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x+3}{3})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{4-(2x-2)^2} \textrm{d}x.$
solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{4-(2x-2)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\int \dfrac{1}{4-4(x-1)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - (x-1)^2 }\textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = x-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(x-1)}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $\left|{x-1} \right| >   1.$

problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}}.$
solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-4{(x-1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x-1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|6x-2|\sqrt{9+(3x-1)^{2}}}.$
solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|6x-2|\sqrt{9+(3x-1)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{9+9{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{1}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x-\frac{1}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{3x-1}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}}.$
solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-9{(x+1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}.$

problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x.$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+3}{2}|>1.$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{3-2x-x^2} \textrm{d}x=$
solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3-2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 + 2x - 3)\\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 + 2\cdot x +1^2 - 1^2 - 3)\\[5pt]
& = -((x+1)^2 - 4) \\[5pt]
&= 4 - (x+1)^2
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{3-2x-x^2}\textrm{d}x =
\int \dfrac{1}{4-(x+1)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - \left( \frac{1}{2}(x+1)\right)^2 }\textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = \dfrac{1}{2}(x+1)$. Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x+1))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x+1))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $\left|\dfrac {x+1} {2} \right| >   1$.

problem:
Solve the equation $x^2 -10x = -24.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that $x^2 -10x +25$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
x^2 -10x +25 = (x-5)^2.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x & =-24 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 5\cdot x & =-24 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 5\cdot x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =-24 \\ (x-5)^{2}-25 & =-24\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we isolate the perfect square by adding $25$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-5)^{2}-25+25 & =-24+25 \\ (x-5)^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-5)^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(x-5)^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ |x-5| & =1 \\ x-5 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =5\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =5-1=4 \\ {x}_{2} & =5+1=6\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Let ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ be the solutions of the equation ${x}^{2}-2x=24.$ Find the value ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}-2x+1$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}-2x+1=(x-1)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x & =24 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x & =24 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2} & =24 \\ (x-1)^{2}-1 & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we isolate the perfect square by adding $1$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}-1+1 & =24+1 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =25 \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{25} \\ |x-1| & =5 \\ x-1 & =\pm 5 \\ x & =1\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =1-5=-4 \\ {x}_{2} & =1+5=6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=(-4)^{2}+{6}^{2}=52.
$$

Let ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ be the solutions of the equation ${x}^{2}+4x=12.$ Find the value ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}+4x+4$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}+4x+4=(x+2)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x & =12 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot x & =12 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =12 \\ (x+2)^{2}-4 & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we isolate the perfect square by adding $4$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{2}-4+4 & =12+4 \\ (x+2)^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{2} & =16 \\ \sqrt{(x+2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{16} \\ |x+2| & =4 \\ x+2 & =\pm 4 \\ x & =-2\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-2-4=-6 \\ {x}_{2} & =-2+4=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=(-6)^{2}+{2}^{2}=40.
$$

$$

$$

problem: Write the equation $x^2 + 6x +5= 0$ in the form $(x+p)^2=q,$ and hence solve the equation.
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+5 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+6x & =-5 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x & =-5 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2} & =-5 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2})-9 & =-5 \\ (x+3)^{2}-9 & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}-9 & =-5 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =-5+9 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, $p=3$ and $q=4$. Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =4 \\ \sqrt{(x+3)^{2}} & =\sqrt{4} \\ |x+3| & =2 \\ x+3 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =-3\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-3+2=-1 \\ {x}_{2} & =-3-2=-5\end{aligned}
$$

problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-4x+4=9$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and the sum of the roots ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+4 & =9 \\ {x}^{2}-4x & =5 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x & =5 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =5 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2})-4 & =5 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}-4 & =5 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-2,q=9,$ and $p+q=7.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =9 \\ \sqrt{(x-2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{9} \\ x-2 & =\pm 3 \\ x & =2\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2+3=5 \\ {x}_{2} & =2-3=-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=5.$ Thus, the sum is $4.$

problem: The equation ${x}^{2}+8x-33=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+8x-33 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+8x & =33 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot x & =33 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot x+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2} & =33 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot x+{4}^{2})-16 & =33 \\ (x+4)^{2}-16 & =33\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square and solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)^{2}-16 & =33 \\ (x+4)^{2} & =49\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=4,q=49,$ and $p+q=53.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)^{2} & =49 \\ \sqrt{(x+4)^{2}} & =\sqrt{49} \\ x+4 & =\pm 7 \\ x & =-4\pm 7\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-4+7=3 \\ x & =-4-7=-11\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-11$ and $x=3.$

problem: The equation ${x}^{2}+6x+8=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q$. Find $\,p+q$, and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+8 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+6x & =-8 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x & =-8 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2} & =-8 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2})-9 & =-8 \\ (x+3)^{2}-9 & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square and solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}-9 & =-8 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=3,q=1$, and $p+q=4$.

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(x+3)^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ x+3 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =-3\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-3+1=-2 \\ x & =-3-1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-4$ and $x=-2$.

problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-20x-21=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q$. Find $\,p+q$, and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-20x-21 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-20x & =21 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 10\cdot x & =21 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 10\cdot x+{10}^{2}-{10}^{2} & =21 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 10\cdot x+{10}^{2})-100 & =21 \\ (x-10)^{2}-100 & =21\end{aligned}

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-10)^{2}-100 & =21 \\ (x-10)^{2} & =121\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-10,q=121$, and $p+q=111$.

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-10)^{2} & =121 \\ \sqrt{(x-10)^{2}} & =\sqrt{121} \\ x-10 & =\pm 11 \\ x & =10\pm 11\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =10+11=21 \\ x & =10-11=-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-1$ and $x=21$.

problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-4x+4=1$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p-q,$ and the sum of the roots ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$
solution:
First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+4 & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot x\cdot 2+{2}^{2} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-2,q=1,$ and $p-q=-3.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(x-2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ x-2 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =2\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2+1=3 \\ {x}_{2} & =2-1=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are ${x}_{1}=3$ and ${x}_{2}=1.$ Thus, the sum is $4.$

problem: The equation ${a}^{2}+8a=9$ can be written in the form $(a+p)^{2}=q$. Find $\,p+q$, and solve the equation.
solution:

problem: The equation ${t}^{2}-14t+5=5$ can be written in the form $(t+p)^{2}=q$. Find $\,pq\,$, and the sum of the roots ${t}_{1}+{t}_{2}$.

problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-2x+1=1$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,pq\,,$ and the sum of the roots ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$

problem: Solve the equation $x^2-2x-1=0.$

problem:
We can use the method of completing the square to solve *any* quadratic equation, even if the equation does not factor.

To illustrate, suppose we want to solve the following equation:

$$
x^2+2x-8=0
$$

We can do so by following the five steps below:

**Step 1.** Move the constant term to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x-8 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x & =8\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x & =8 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot x & =8 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2} & =8 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot x+{1}^{2})-1 & =8 \\ (x+1)^{2}-1 & =8\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Isolate the perfect square by adding $1$ to both sides. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2} & =9 \\ \sqrt{(x+1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{9} \\ |x+1| & =3 \\ x+1 & =\pm 3 \\ x & =-1\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5.** Finally, we simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-1-3=-4 \\ {x}_{2} & =-1+3=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-4$ and $x=2.$
Find the center and the lengths of the major and minor axes of the ellipse whose equation is $25x^2 + 9y^2 - 100x - 18y = 116.$
solution:
First, we must group the $x$ terms and the $y$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}25{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}-100x-18y & =116 \\ (25{x}^{2}-100x)+(9{y}^{2}-18y) & =116\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the both the $x$ and $y$ terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(25{x}^{2}-100x)+(9{y}^{2}-18y) & =116 \\ 25[{x}^{2}-4x]+9[{y}^{2}-2y] & =116 \\ 25[(x-2)^{2}-4]+9[(y-1)^{2}-1] & =116 \\ 25(x-2)^{2}-100+9(y-1)^{2}-9 & =116\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rearrange the equation into the desired form:

$$
\begin{aligned}25(x-2)^{2}-100+9(y-1)^{2}-9 & =116 \\ 25(x-2)^{2}+9(y-1)^{2} & =116+100+9 \\ 25(x-2)^{2}+9(y-1)^{2} & =225 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $5 > 3,$ the length of the major axis is $2\cdot 5 =10,$ the length of the minor axis is $2\cdot 3 =6,$ and the ellipse is centered at $({2},{1}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{x}^{2}+12x)+({y}^{2}-4y) & =-20 \\ 2({x}^{2}+6x)+({y}^{2}-4y) & =-20 \\ 2[(x+3)^{2}-9]+[(y-2)^{2}-4] & =-20 \\ 2(x+3)^{2}-18+(y-2)^{2}-4 & =-20\end{aligned}

$$

problem: Determine  the lengths of the major and minor axes of the ellipse whose equation is ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-4x+16y=-16.$
solution:
First, we must group the $x$ terms and the $y$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-4x+16y & =-16 \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+(4{y}^{2}+16y) & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must complete the square for both the $x$ and $y$ terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}-4x)+(4{y}^{2}+16y) & =-16 \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+4({y}^{2}+4y) & =-16 \\ [(x-2)^{2}-4]+4[(y+2)^{2}-4] & =-16 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4+4(y+2)^{2}-16 & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rearrange the equation into the desired form:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}-4+4(y+2)^{2}-16 & =-16 \\ (x-2)^{2}+4(y+2)^{2} & =-16+16+4 \\ (x-2)^{2}+4(y+2)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{1} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2>1,$ the length of the major axis is $2\cdot 2=4,$ and the length of the minor axis is $2\cdot 1=2.$

$$

$$

Now, we complete the square for the both the $x$ and $y$ terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}-6x)+(4{y}^{2}+24y)+41 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-6x)+4[{y}^{2}+6y]+41 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2}-9+4[(y+3)^{2}-9]+41 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2}-9+4(y+3)^{2}-36+41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rearrange the equation into the desired form:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2}-9+4(y+3)^{2}-36+41 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2}+4(y+3)^{2} & =9+36-41 \\ (x-3)^{2}+4(y+3)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{1} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}

Since $2 > 1,$ the length of the major axis is $2\cdot 2 =4,$ the length of the minor axis is $2\cdot 1 =2,$ and the ellipse is centered at $({3},{-3}).$

$$

$$

$$

Consider the integral

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-10x+34}}\, \textrm{d}x
$$

As it is, this integral doesn't resemble any of the basic integrals we have encountered so far. However, we can complete the square for the denominator, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 10x + 34 &= x^{2} - 10x + (25 - 25) + 34 \\
&= (x^{2} - 10x + 25) - 25 + 34 \\
&= (x - 5)^{2} + 9
\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug the above into our integral and collect a factor of $9$ in the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 10x + 34}}dx &= \int\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{(x - 5)^{2} + 9}} \\
&= \int\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{9[\frac{(x - 5)^{2}}{9} + 1]}} \\
&= \frac{1}{3}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{(\frac{x - 5}{3})^{2} + 1}}
\end{aligned}
$$

This now looks more familiar! Let

$$
u = \dfrac {x-5}{3}
$$

Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = 3\,\textrm{d}u
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 10x + 34}}dx &= \frac{1}{3}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{(\frac{x - 5}{3})^{2} + 1}} \\
&= \frac{1}{3}\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{u^{2} + 1}} \cdot (3du) \\
&= \int\frac{1}{\sqrt{u^{2} + 1}}du
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a basic integral for an inverse hyperbolic function, and we can solve it in one step:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{u^{2} + 1}}du &= \operatorname{arsinh} u + C \\
&= \operatorname{arsinh} (\frac{x - 5}{3}) + C
\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Let's recall the formula for factoring a perfect square:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}}x + a^2 = (x + {\color{blue}{a}})^2
$$

As we've seen, **completing the square** on a quadratic expression means expressing it as the sum of a perfect square and a constant.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to complete the square on a quadratic expression when the coefficient of the linear term is odd. In these cases, we get a fraction in the final expression.

As an example, let's consider the following quadratic expression:

$$
\left(x^2 + 5x + \left(\dfrac 52\right)^2\right) + 1
$$

Notice that we have a perfect square in the large parentheses that we can factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& {x}^{2}+5x+{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2} \\
&= {x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{5}{2}x+{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2} \\
&= {(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our original expression can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see another example.

Let's complete the square on the following expression: 

$$
x^2 + 3x + 4
$$

The procedure is very similar to the one we encountered when the coefficient of the linear term was even.

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}x + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

Now, here's the trick. We *add* and *then subtract* $\left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2$, writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{4}}$ last:

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}x  + \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 - \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

As a result, the first three terms now form a perfect square!

$$
\underbrace{x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}x  + \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2} - \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

Factoring the perfect square, we get

$$
\left(x + {\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2  - \left({\color{blue}{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right)^2 + {\color{purple}{4}}.
$$

Finally, evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& {(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+4 \\
&= {(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}+4 \\
&= {(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}+\frac{16}{4} \\
&= {(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+\frac{7}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Write the equation $2x^2 - 6x = 1$ in the form $(x+p)^2 = q,$ and hence solve the equation.
solution:
First, we divide out by the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-6x & =1 \\ 2({x}^{2}-3x) & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-3x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot (\frac{3}{2})\cdot x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =\frac{2}{4} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{11}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-\dfrac32$ and $q=\dfrac{11}{4}.$ Now, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{4}} \\ |x-\frac{3}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{2} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{3\pm \sqrt{11}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: The equation $5{x}^{2}+2x-3=0$ can be written in the form $5(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q-p.$
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{2}+2x-3 & =0 \\ 5{x}^{2}+2x & =3 \\ 5{x}^{2}+2x & =3 \\ 5({x}^{2}+\frac{2}{5}x) & =3 \\ 5[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{5}x+{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}] & =3 \\ 5[{(x+\frac{1}{5})}^{2}-\frac{1}{25}] & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{(x+\frac{1}{5})}^{2}-5\cdot \frac{1}{25} & =3 \\ 5{(x+\frac{1}{5})}^{2}-\frac{1}{5} & =3 \\ 5{(x+\frac{1}{5})}^{2} & =3+\frac{1}{5} \\ 5{(x+\frac{1}{5})}^{2} & =\frac{16}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{1}{5}$ and $q=\frac{16}{5}.$ Finally,

$$
q-p=\frac{16}{5}-\frac{1}{5}=\frac{15}{5}=3.
$$

problem: The equation $2{x}^{2}-4x-9=0$ can be written in the form $2(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-4x-9 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-4x & =9 \\ 2({x}^{2}-2x) & =9 \\ 2[{x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x+{(1)}^{2}-{(1)}^{2}] & =9 \\ 2[{(x-1)}^{2}-1] & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x-1)}^{2}-2\cdot 1 & =9 \\ 2{(x-1)}^{2}-2 & =9 \\ 2{(x-1)}^{2} & =9+2 \\ 2{(x-1)}^{2} & =11\end{aligned}
$$

So, $q=11.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x-1)}^{2} & =11 \\ {(x-1)}^{2} & =\frac{11}{2} \\ \sqrt{{(x-1)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ |x-1| & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ x-1 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ x & =1\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: The equation $6{z}^{2}+10z-1=0$ can be written in the form $6(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q.$
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}6{z}^{2}+10z-1 & =0 \\ 6{z}^{2}+10z & =1 \\ 6({z}^{2}+\frac{5}{3}z) & =1 \\ 6[{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{5}{6}\cdot z+{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}] & =1 \\ 6[{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2}] & =1 \\ 6[{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-\frac{25}{36}] & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-6\cdot \frac{25}{36} & =1 \\ 6{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2}-\frac{25}{6} & =1 \\ 6{(z+\frac{5}{6})}^{2} & =\frac{31}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{5}{6}$ and $q=\frac{31}{6}.$ Finally,

$$
p+q=\frac{5}{6}+\frac{31}{6}=\frac{36}{6}=6.
$$

problem: The equation $4{z}^{2}+4z=12$ can be written in the form $(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, divide it by the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}+4z & =12 \\ 4({z}^{2}+z) & =12 \\ {z}^{2}+z & =3 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot z & =3 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\cdot z+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{12}{4} \\ {(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{13}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=\frac{1}{2},q=\frac{13}{4},$ and $p+q=\frac{15}{4}.$ 

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(z+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{13}{4}} \\ |z+\frac{1}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z+\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z & =-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2} \\ z & =\frac{-1\pm \sqrt{13}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: The equation $3{z}^{2}-15=12z$ can be written in the form $(z-p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, divide it by the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{2}-15 & =12z \\ 3{z}^{2}-12z & =15 \\ 3({z}^{2}-4z) & =15 \\ {z}^{2}-4z & =5 \\ {z}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot z & =5 \\ {z}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot z+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =5 \\ {(z-2)}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z-2)}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =5 \\ {(z-2)}^{2}-4 & =5 \\ {(z-2)}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=2$ and $q=9.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(z-2)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{9} \\ |z-2| & =3 \\ z-2 & =\pm 3 \\ z & =2\pm 3 \\ z & =-1,\,5\end{aligned}
$$

problem: The equation $2{z}^{2}+4z=10$  can be written in the form $(z+p)^{2}+q=0.$ Find $p,$ and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we divide out by the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{z}^{2}+4z & =10 \\ 2({z}^{2}+2z) & =10 \\ {z}^{2}+2z & =5 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot z & =5 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot z+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2} & =5 \\ {(z+1)}^{2}-{1}^{2} & =5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z+1)}^{2}-{1}^{2} & =5 \\ {(z+1)}^{2}-1 & =5 \\ {(z+1)}^{2}-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, $p=1$ and $q=-6.$ 

Now, let's solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+1)^{2}-6 & =0 \\ (z+1)^{2} & =6 \\ \sqrt{(z+1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{6} \\ |z+1| & =\sqrt{6} \\ z+1 & =\pm \sqrt{6} \\ z & =-1\pm \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: The equation $3{x}^{2}-4x+1=0$ can be written in the form $3(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q.$
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-4x+1 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4x & =-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4x & =-1 \\ 3({x}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}x) & =-1 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{2}{3}x+{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}] & =-1 \\ 3[{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}-\frac{4}{9}] & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}-3\cdot \frac{4}{9} & =-1 \\ 3{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}-\frac{4}{3} & =-1 \\ 3{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2} & =-1+\frac{4}{3} \\ 3{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-\frac{2}{3}$ and $q=\frac{1}{3}.$

problem: The equation $2{x}^{2}+10x+12=0$ can be written in the form $2(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p,$ and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side,  factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+10x+12 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}+10x & =-12 \\ 2{x}^{2}+10x & =-12 \\ 2({x}^{2}+5x) & =-12 \\ 2[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{5}{2}x+{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}] & =-12 \\ 2[{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-\frac{25}{4}] & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{25}{4} & =-12 \\ 2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-\frac{25}{2} & =-12 \\ 2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =-12+\frac{25}{2} \\ 2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{5}{2}.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(x+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\ |x+\frac{5}{2}| & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x+\frac{5}{2} & =\pm \frac{1}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{5}{2}\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{6}{3}=-3 \\ x & =-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{4}{2}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-3$ and $x=-2.$

problem: The equation $4{x}^{2}-6x-3=0$ can be written in the form $4(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p,$ and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-6x-3 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}-6x & =3 \\ 4[{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}x] & =3 \\ 4[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{4}x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =3 \\ 4[{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =3 \\ 4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =3 \\ 4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =3+\frac{9}{4} \\ 4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{21}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-\frac{3}{4}.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{21}{4} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{21}{16} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{21}{16}} \\ |x-\frac{3}{4}| & =\sqrt{\frac{21}{16}} \\ x-\frac{3}{4} & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{21}{16}} \\ x-\frac{3}{4} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{21}}{4} \\ x & =\frac{3}{4}\pm \frac{\sqrt{21}}{4} \\ x & =\frac{3\pm \sqrt{21}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: The equation $4{x}^{2}+6x-5=0$ can be written in the form $4(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q.$
solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+6x-5 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x) & =5 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =5 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =5 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{29}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{4}$ and $q=\frac{29}{4}.$ Finally,

$$
p+q=\frac{3}{4}+\frac{29}{4}=\frac{32}{4}=8.
$$

problem: The equation $3{z}^{2}-12=9z$ can be written in the form $(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation.
solution:
First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{2}-12 & =9z \\ 3{z}^{2}-9z-12 & =0 \\ 3({z}^{2}-3z-4) & =0 \\ {z}^{2}-3z-4 & =0 \\ {z}^{2}-2\cdot z\cdot \frac{3}{2} & =4 \\ {z}^{2}-2\cdot z\cdot \frac{3}{2}+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =-4 \\ [{z}^{2}-2\cdot z\cdot \frac{3}{2}+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}]-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =-4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{25}{4} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-\frac{3}{2},q=\frac{25}{4}$ and $p+q=\frac{19}{4}.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |z-\frac{3}{2}| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ z-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ z & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{5}{2}=4 \\ z & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $z=4$ and $z=-1.$

problem: Write the equation $-2x^2+2x+1 = 0$ in the form $2(x+p)^2=q,$ and hence solve the equation.
solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-2{x}^{2}+2x+1) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2x-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

problem: The equation $-5{x}^{2}+5x-1=0$ can be written in the form $5(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q.$

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{2}-5x+1 & =0 \\ 5{x}^{2}-5x & =-1 \\ 5({x}^{2}-x) & =-1 \\ 5[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =-1 \\ 5[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =-1\end{aligned}

problem:
Solve the equation $-2x^2 - 4x = 1.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that $x^2 + 2x + 1$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
x^2 + 2x + 1 = (x + 1)^2.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}-4x & =1 \\ -2({x}^{2}+2x) & =1 \\ -2({x}^{2}+2\cdot 1x) & =1 \\ -2({x}^{2}+2\cdot 1x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =1 \\ -2[(x+1)^{2}-{1}^{2}] & =1 \\ -2[(x+1)^{2}-1] & =1 \\ -2(x+1)^{2}+(-2)(-1) & =1 \\ -2(x+1)^{2}+2 & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $2$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-2),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2(x+1)^{2}+2 & =1 \\ -2(x+1)^{2}+2-2 & =1-2 \\ -2(x+1)^{2} & =-1 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =\frac{(-1)}{(-2)} \\ (x+1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{(x+1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\ |x+1| & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ x+1 & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ x & =-1\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Solve the equation $5{y}^{2}-40y=-76.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${y}^{2}-8y+16$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{y}^{2}-8y+16=(y-4)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2}-40y & =-76 \\ 5({y}^{2}-8y) & =-76 \\ 5({y}^{2}-2\cdot 4y) & =-76 \\ 5({y}^{2}-2\cdot 4y+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2}) & =-76 \\ 5[(y-4)^{2}-{4}^{2}] & =-76 \\ 5[(y-4)^{2}-16] & =-76 \\ 5(y-4)^{2}-80 & =-76\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $80$ to both sides and then dividing by $5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5(y-4)^{2}-80 & =-76 \\ 5(y-4)^{2}-80+80 & =-76+80 \\ 5(y-4)^{2} & =4 \\ (y-4)^{2} & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-4)^{2} & =\frac{4}{5} \\ \sqrt{(y-4)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{5}} \\ |y-4| & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ y-4 & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ y & =4\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Solve the equation $-6{y}^{2}+24y=21.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${y}^{2}-4y+4$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{y}^{2}-4y+4=(y-2)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6{y}^{2}+24y & =21 \\ -6({y}^{2}-4y) & =21 \\ -6({y}^{2}-2\cdot 2y) & =21 \\ -6({y}^{2}-2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}) & =21 \\ -6[(y-2)^{2}-{2}^{2}] & =21 \\ -6[(y-2)^{2}-4] & =21 \\ -6(y-2)^{2}+(-6)(-4) & =21 \\ -6(y-2)^{2}+24 & =21\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $24$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-6),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6(y-2)^{2}+24 & =21 \\ -6(y-2)^{2}+24-24 & =21-24 \\ -6(y-2)^{2} & =-3 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =\frac{(-3)}{(-6)} \\ (y-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{(y-2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\ |y-2| & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ y-2 & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ y & =2\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Solve the equation $-7{y}^{2}-42y=62.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${y}^{2}+6y+9$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{y}^{2}+6y+9=(y+3)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}-7{y}^{2}-42y & =62 \\ -7({y}^{2}+6y) & =62 \\ -7({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y) & =62 \\ -7({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) & =62 \\ -7[(y+3)^{2}-{3}^{2}] & =62 \\ -7[(y+3)^{2}-9] & =62 \\ -7(y+3)^{2}+(-7)(-9) & =62 \\ -7(y+3)^{2}+63 & =62\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $63$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-7),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-7(y+3)^{2}+63 & =62 \\ -7(y+3)^{2}+63-63 & =62-63 \\ -7(y+3)^{2} & =-1 \\ (y+3)^{2} & =\frac{(-1)}{(-7)} \\ (y+3)^{2} & =\frac{1}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =\frac{1}{7} \\ \sqrt{(y+3)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{7}} \\ |y+3| & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \\ y+3 & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \\ y & =-3\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Solve the equation $-4{x}^{2}+4x=-2.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}={(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}+4x & =-2 \\ -4({x}^{2}-x) & =-2 \\ -4({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x) & =-2 \\ -4({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =-2 \\ -4[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =-2 \\ -4[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =-2 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(-4)(-\frac{1}{4}) & =-2 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1 & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $1$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-4),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1 & =-2 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1-1 & =-2-1 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =-3 \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{(-3)}{(-4)} \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\ |x-\frac{1}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x-\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Solve the equation $4{x}^{2}+24x=-11.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}+6x+9$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}+6x+9=(x+3)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+24x & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+6x) & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x) & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) & =-11 \\ 4[(x+3)^{2}-{3}^{2}] & =-11 \\ 4[(x+3)^{2}-9] & =-11 \\ 4(x+3)^{2}-36 & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $36$ to both sides and then dividing by $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x+3)^{2}-36 & =-11 \\ 4(x+3)^{2}-36+36 & =-11+36 \\ 4(x+3)^{2} & =25 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x+3)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |x+3| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ x+3 & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-3\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{11}{2},\,-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Solve the equation $4{x}^{2}-8x=5.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}-2x+1$ is a perfect square.*
solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}-2x+1=(x-1)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-8x & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2x) & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x) & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =5 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =5 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $4$ to both sides and then dividing by $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =5 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4+4 & =5+4 \\ 4(x-1)^{2} & =9 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} \\ |x-1| & =\frac{3}{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \frac{3}{2} \\ x & =1\pm \frac{3}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Solve the equation $9{x}^{2}-18x=7.$  Write the solutions in ascending order.

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}-2x+1$ is a perfect square.*

solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}-2x+1=(x-1)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-18x & =7 \\ 9({x}^{2}-2x) & =7 \\ 9({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x) & =7 \\ 9({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1y+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =7 \\ 9[(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}] & =7 \\ 9[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =7 \\ 9(x-1)^{2}-9 & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $9$ to both sides and then dividing by $9$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9(x-1)^{2}-9 & =7 \\ 9(x-1)^{2}-9+9 & =7+9 \\ 9(x-1)^{2} & =16 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{16}{9}.\end{aligned}

$$

problem:
We can use the method of completing the square to solve quadratic equations with leading coefficients. 

As an example, let's solve the following quadratic equation by completing the square:

$$
4x^2-8x+3 = 0
$$

First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-8x+3 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}-8x & =-3 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2x) & =-3 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =-3 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, expanding the brackets, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =-3 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we isolate the perfect square by adding  $4$ to both sides and then dividing by $4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =-3 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4+4 & =-3+4 \\ 4(x-1)^{2} & =1 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\ |x-1| & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \frac{1}{2} \\ x & =1\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\dfrac12$ and $x=\dfrac32.$

Consider the quadratic equation

$$
ax^2+bx+c = 0,
$$

where $a\neq 0.$ We can derive a general solution to this equation by completing the square.

First, let's subtract $c$ from both sides to isolate the variable terms:

$$
ax^2+bx = -c
$$

Since $a\neq 0,$ dividing by $a$ gives

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{b}{a}x = -\dfrac{c}{a}.
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side and move the constant terms to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{b}{2a}x=-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-{(\frac{b}{2a})}^{2} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2}-\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{c}{a} \\ {(x+\frac{b}{2a})}^{2} & =\frac{{b}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}}-\frac{c}{a}\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the terms on the right-hand side over a common factor of $4a^2,$ we get

$$
\left(x + \dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2  = \dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}.
$$

Taking the square root of both sides yields

$$
x + \dfrac{b}{2a}  = \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}}
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{b}{2a} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we isolate $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{b}{2a}\pm \frac{\sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies as

$$
x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.
$$

This formula is called the **quadratic formula**. You'll learn more about how to apply the quadratic formula in future lessons.
Rewrite $-x^2+6x+1$ by completing the square.
solution:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $-1.$ So, we take out a factor of $-1$ from the entire expression:

$$
-(x^2 - 6x -1)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
x^2 - 6x - {\color{purple}{1}}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with ${\color{red}{2}}$ as a factor:

$$
x^2 - {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{3}}x - {\color{purple}{1}}
$$

Then, we add and then subtract ${\color{blue}{3}}^2,$ writing the constant term ${\color{purple}{1}}$ last:

$$
\underbrace{x^2 - {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{3}}x + {\color{blue}{3}}^2} - {\color{blue}{3}}^2 - {\color{purple}{1}}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
(x-{\color{blue}{3}})^2 - {\color{blue}{3}}^2- {\color{purple}{1}}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
(x-{\color{blue}{3}})^2 - 10
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+6x+1 & =-((x-3)^{2}-10) \\  & =-(x-3)^{2}+10 \\  & =10-(x-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Rewrite $-({k}^{2}-16k+8)$ by completing the square.
solution:
We begin by completing the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{k}^{2}-16k+8
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{k}^{2}-2\cdot 8k+8
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${8}^{2}$, writing the constant term $8$ last:

$$
\underbrace{{k}^{2}-2\cdot 8k+{8}^{2}}-{8}^{2}+8
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
(k-8)^{2}-{8}^{2}+8
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
(k-8)^{2}-56.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-({k}^{2}-16k+8) & =-({(k-8)}^{2}-56) \\  & =-(k-8)^{2}+56 \\  & =56-(k-8)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

solution:

$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$

$$

$$
{a}^{2}+2\cdot 5a-16
$$

Then, we add and then subtract ${5}^{2}$, writing the constant term $16$ last:

$$
\underbrace{{a}^{2}+2\cdot 5a+{5}^{2}}-{5}^{2}-16
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
(a+5)^{2}-{5}^{2}-16
$$

$$
(a+5)^{2}-41
$$

$$

$$

\underbrace{{x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x+{1}^{2}}-{1}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}

problem: Rewrite $6{x}^{2}-2x$ by completing the square.
solution:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $6$. So, we take out a factor of $6$ from the entire expression:

$$
6({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}x)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}x
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{6}x
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}$: 

$$
\underbrace{{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{6}x+{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}}-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}
$$

Evaluating the last term, we get

$$
{(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-\frac{1}{36}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}6({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}x) & =6({(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-\frac{1}{36}) \\  & =6{(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-6\cdot \frac{1}{36} \\  & =6{(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Rewrite $4{x}^{2}+24x$ by completing the square.
solution:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $4$. So, we take out a factor of $4$ from the entire expression:

$$
4({x}^{2}+6x)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}+6x
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${3}^{2}$:

$$
\underbrace{{x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}}-{3}^{2}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(x+3)}^{2}-{3}^{2}
$$

Evaluating the last term, we get

$$
{(x+3)}^{2}-9.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}^{2}+6x) & =4({(x+3)}^{2}-9) \\  & =4{(x+3)}^{2}-4\cdot 9 \\  & =4{(x+3)}^{2}-36\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{3}}x  + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

$$
\underbrace{x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}\cdot {\color{blue}{3}}x + {\color{blue}{3}}^2} - {\color{blue}{3}}^2 + {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
(x+{\color{blue}{3}})^2 - {\color{blue}{3}}^2+ {\color{purple}{4}}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
(x+{\color{blue}{3}})^2 - 5
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-({x}^{2}+6x+4) & =-((x+3)^{2}-5) \\  & =-(x+3)^{2}+5 \\  & =5-(x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$
